title: Differential Continuity And Monotonicity
notes: Open by connecting the previous section to this one: subgradients are not arbitrary derivative substitutes. Once they come from a closed proper convex function, their graph is ordered, closed, locally bounded on compact cores, and eventually recoverable from cyclic inequalities. The lecture is about reading those facts directly from pictures.

title: Gradient Map Picture
notes: Use the quadratic picture as the smooth calibration case. Two nearby domain points have gradient arrows that turn in the same broad direction as the displacement. The panel on the right makes the map itself visible: the difference of gradients is not a random vector, but the image of the displacement through a positive curvature field.

title: Monotone Inequality
notes: Derive the inequality by writing the two supporting inequalities and adding them. The cancellation is the whole proof. Students should notice that no differentiability is needed: the same line works for any selected subgradients p and q, so monotonicity belongs to the set-valued graph rather than to a smooth formula.

title: Secant Slopes
notes: In one dimension, monotonicity can be seen through secant slopes. As the secant window moves to the right, convexity prevents the slope from decreasing. The left and right derivatives are therefore monotone functions, and the jump between them is exactly where the subdifferential becomes an interval instead of a point.

title: Subgradient Graph
notes: Read the right panel as a graph rather than as a list of formulas. Horizontal pieces record constant slopes on linear stretches, while vertical pieces record all supporting slopes at corners. Filling those vertical pieces is what makes the graph closed and maximal in the one-dimensional order.

title: Maximal Monotone Intuition
notes: The one-dimensional theorem says that subgradient graphs are complete nondecreasing curves. A missing vertical interval would still look monotone locally, but it would fail completeness because another ordered point could be inserted. This is the first geometric hint of maximality, before the higher-dimensional cyclic statement arrives.

title: Continuity On Smooth Regions
notes: Explain continuity of the gradient as a consequence of three ingredients: the graph of the subdifferential is closed, subgradients are locally bounded on compact sets inside the domain, and at a smooth point the subdifferential has only one vector. Any convergent subsequence of gradients must land on that one vector, so the whole gradient sequence converges.

title: Jumps At Corners
notes: The absolute value example prevents students from overgeneralizing smooth behavior. The derivative jumps from minus one to plus one, but the subdifferential at the corner is the whole interval between them. The map is not continuous as a single-valued gradient, yet it is closed and outer-continuous as a set-valued graph.

title: Cyclic Monotonicity Preview
notes: Pairwise monotonicity checks every two-point comparison. Cyclic monotonicity asks for consistency around every finite loop, which is the correct test for being generated by a convex potential. The rotation example is useful because it passes pairwise monotonicity with equality but still creates negative work around a loop.

title: Numerical Monotonicity Matrix
notes: For a linear map, the pairwise test collapses to a matrix test on the symmetric part. A skew component disappears from dot(d,Qd), so it does not harm monotonicity. But cyclic monotonicity is stricter: a linear subgradient map must be symmetric positive semidefinite, matching the Hessian of a convex quadratic.

title: Failure Examples
notes: Collect the traps in one place. A nonclosed convex function can lose derivative limit behavior at the boundary. A graph with a missing jump interval fails closedness and maximality. A rotation field can be monotone without being cyclically monotone. Each failure marks a hypothesis that Section 24 deliberately keeps visible.

title: Rule Ledger
notes: Treat the ledger as an operating manual for the section. To audit a proposed subgradient picture, check pairwise monotonicity, closed graph behavior, local boundedness on compact cores, smooth-region gradient continuity, cyclic loop residuals, and the matrix test when the mapping is linear. These checks reinforce each other rather than standing alone.

title: Graphical Checks
notes: Move from theorem statements to inspection habits. A good graph should reveal increasing order, filled vertical jumps, bounded slope range on interior windows, and no negative cycle residual. When one of those features is absent, the visual should tell students which theorem or qualification has stopped applying.

title: Recap
notes: Close by tying the lecture back to the larger differential theory. Subgradient maps behave like generalized gradients because convexity forces their graph to be ordered and closed. Smooth regions recover continuous gradients; corners become vertical intervals; cyclic monotonicity identifies exactly the maps that can come from convex potentials.
